title: Health as a capital stock
prompt: In a Grossman-style model, what distinguishes health capital from a medical visit?
correct: Health capital produces services over time; a visit is an input that may affect that stock.
wrong: Each visit is itself the entire health stock.
Only purchased care can produce health.
explanation: A stock of health yields healthy time and consumption benefits. Medical care is one possible investment input, alongside time and other resources.
hint: Separate a durable stock from an input used to maintain it.

title: Health stock transition
prompt: A hypothetical health stock is 100. During the year 10% depreciates and investment adds 15 stock units. Under H_next=(1−δ)H+I, what is next year’s stock?
explanation: The surviving stock is 90; adding investment of 15 gives 105. Investment is added after depreciation under the stated equation.
hint: Compute the surviving stock first.

title: Replacement investment
prompt: A hypothetical person wants to maintain health stock H=80 with annual depreciation δ=0.15. How much investment is required under H_next=(1−δ)H+I?
correct: 12 stock units.
explanation: A constant stock requires I=δH=0.15×80=12. The surviving stock of 68 is not the required investment.
hint: Replace exactly what depreciates.

title: Time price of care
prompt: A hypothetical visit costs a patient $30 and takes two hours including travel. If the opportunity cost of time is $20 per hour, what is the full private cost?
explanation: Full cost is the money price plus time cost: 30+2×20=70. A money price alone omits a scarce input.
hint: Include both money and forgone time.

title: Derived demand
prompt: An innovation delivers the same improvement in health with fewer clinic visits, at unchanged input prices. Which conclusion follows directly?
correct: The visits needed to produce a given health improvement fall.
explanation: The production requirement falls. Desired health and total use may also respond to the lower effective cost, so their final directions are not pinned down.
hint: Hold the target health improvement fixed before considering behavioral responses.

title: Diminishing marginal product
prompt: In a hypothetical production schedule, successive units of care raise a health index by 8, 5, and 2. What does this illustrate?
correct: Positive but diminishing marginal product of care.
wrong: Zero productivity of the third unit.
explanation: Each extra unit still improves the index, but by less than the previous unit. Diminishing returns do not mean negative returns.
hint: Compare increments rather than the accumulated index.

title: Investment return and depreciation
prompt: In a stylized interior health-investment model with marginal return schedule fixed and downward sloping in H, equilibrium satisfies R(H)=r+δ. What happens to desired H when δ rises?
correct: Desired H falls.
wrong: Desired H is unchanged for every schedule.
Desired H becomes equal to δ.
explanation: Higher depreciation raises the required return. A downward-sloping R(H) reaches that higher return at a smaller stock. This holds under the fixed-schedule assumptions.
hint: Move up along a downward-sloping return schedule.

title: Healthy time and wages
prompt: In the investment component of a health-capital model, a higher wage raises the value of an extra healthy hour available for work. What is this channel?
correct: A higher monetary return to health investment.
wrong: A reduction in the value of healthy time.
Proof that health investment must rise after all effects.
A fall in the opportunity cost of time spent producing health.
explanation: The earnings benefit of healthy time rises. Higher wages can also raise time-input costs; the isolated return channel does not settle the overall effect.
hint: Distinguish the return channel from the cost of time inputs.

title: Price elasticity of visits
prompt: At a hypothetical price of $50 and quantity of 20 visits, demand has derivative dQ/dP=−0.2. What is the point price elasticity?
explanation: Point elasticity is (dQ/dP)(P/Q)=−0.2×50/20=−0.5. The slope alone has units and is not an elasticity.
hint: Multiply the slope by price divided by quantity.

title: Health and care correlation
prompt: A hypothetical survey finds that people receiving more medical care have worse health. What prevents interpreting this as proof that care causes worse health?
correct: Poor underlying health may increase demand for care.
wrong: A negative correlation always proves beneficial treatment.
Care use is necessarily randomly assigned.
Reverse causality is impossible for health outcomes.
explanation: Illness can cause both poor observed health and higher utilization. The association does not isolate a treatment effect.
hint: Consider why people seek care.

title: Actuarially fair premium
prompt: A hypothetical policy fully covers a $10,000 loss that occurs with probability 0.08. Ignore behavior changes and administrative costs. What premium equals expected claims?
explanation: Expected claims are 0.08×10,000=800. Fairness here refers to expected payouts, not every consumer’s willingness to pay.
hint: Weight the loss by its probability.

title: Risk aversion and full insurance
prompt: A person has strictly concave utility of wealth, faces a nondegenerate monetary medical loss, and can buy full coverage at its expected loss with no behavior change. Why prefer full coverage to remaining uninsured?
correct: It removes wealth risk without changing expected wealth.
wrong: It raises expected wealth by the full loss.
Concavity makes uncertain wealth preferable at the same mean.
It guarantees that no illness occurs.
explanation: Jensen’s inequality implies that certain wealth is preferred to a lottery with the same mean under strict concavity. Insurance covers financial loss, not the occurrence of illness.
hint: Compare wealth distributions at equal expected wealth.

title: Independent risk pooling
prompt: A pool contains 100 independent people whose annual claims each have standard deviation $1,000. What is the standard deviation of average claims per person?
explanation: For independent equal-variance claims, divide the individual standard deviation by the square root of the pool size: 1,000/√100=100. Total claims instead have standard deviation 10,000.
hint: The question asks about the average, not the total.

title: Correlated claims
prompt: Two insurance pools have identical individual claim distributions and size, but one has positively correlated claims. Relative to independent claims, what does positive covariance do to the variance of average claims?
correct: It increases the variance.
explanation: The variance of the average contains covariance terms. Positive covariance makes pooling less effective at smoothing financial risk without itself changing marginal means.
hint: Expand the variance of a sum.

title: Deductible and coinsurance
prompt: A hypothetical annual plan has a $500 deductible followed by 20% patient coinsurance, with no other provisions. For $1,500 of covered spending and no prior spending, what does the patient pay?
explanation: The patient pays the first 500 plus 20% of the remaining 1,000: 500+200=700. Applying coinsurance to the full bill overlooks the deductible sequence.
hint: Apply the deductible before coinsurance.

title: Selection into a common premium
prompt: At a hypothetical common premium, people who privately know they have higher expected claims are more likely to enroll. Which mechanism is present?
correct: Adverse selection.
explanation: Enrollment is correlated with private information about expected costs. Moral hazard instead concerns behavior affected by coverage.
hint: Is coverage changing behavior or sorting pre-existing risk?

title: Ex post moral hazard
prompt: A randomly assigned reduction in a visit copayment raises visits while covered populations remain otherwise comparable. Which insurance mechanism does this illustrate?
correct: Ex post moral hazard through a lower marginal price of care.
wrong: A mechanical increase in medical need.
Risk pooling with no behavioral response.
explanation: Conditional on comparable risk, lower cost sharing changes utilization after coverage is in place. The label does not establish whether extra care is valuable.
hint: Focus on behavior after the patient price changes.

title: Insurance welfare tradeoff
prompt: Why is evidence that insurance increases utilization insufficient by itself to show that insurance reduces welfare?
correct: Financial risk protection and the benefits and costs of additional care also matter.
wrong: All additional utilization has zero benefit.
Insurance premiums are always pure social losses.
Any utilization response proves adverse selection.
explanation: Insurance can smooth consumption while changing care decisions. A welfare assessment needs those gains and the resource costs and benefits of additional use.
hint: Consider insurance’s purpose as well as its effect on utilization.

title: Pooling premium and exit
prompt: A hypothetical pool has 80 low-risk members with expected claims $1,000 each and 20 high-risk members with expected claims $5,000 each. With no loading, what common premium covers expected claims?
explanation: Average claims are (80×1,000+20×5,000)/100=1,800. The unweighted average of the two risk types incorrectly gives each type half the pool.
hint: Weight costs by enrollment shares.

title: Risk adjustment
prompt: An insurer receives larger prospective transfers for enrollees with higher predicted costs. What is the intended selection-related effect of accurate risk adjustment?
correct: Reduce the financial incentive to avoid high-cost enrollees.
wrong: Eliminate all uncertainty in realized claims.
Require high-risk people to receive less coverage.
explanation: Matching payments to predictable costs can reduce profit differences across risk types. Prediction error and imperfect incentives may remain.
hint: Ask which enrollment incentives predictable cost differences create.

title: Fee-for-service margin
prompt: A hypothetical clinic receives $90 for an extra visit and incurs $60 in incremental cost. Ignoring other effects, what is the visit’s contribution to profit?
explanation: Contribution is incremental revenue minus incremental cost: 90−60=30. Fixed costs do not change this marginal calculation.
hint: Compare the revenue and cost caused by the extra visit.

title: Capitation and marginal revenue
prompt: A clinic receives a fixed monthly payment per enrolled person, independent of visits. For an additional visit by an existing enrollee, what is the direct marginal payment under this contract?
explanation: Capitation pays for enrollment rather than each visit. Additional visits can affect outcomes and future enrollment, but do not directly generate another payment under the stated rule.
hint: Hold enrollment and the monthly contract fixed.

title: Salary contract
prompt: A salaried clinician receives the same pay for 15 or 16 visits in a day. Which statement follows from the compensation rule alone?
correct: The sixteenth visit produces no additional salary payment.
wrong: The clinician will never provide a sixteenth visit.
Quality must be higher than under fee-for-service.
The sixteenth visit has no social benefit.
explanation: A fixed salary removes a direct payment margin but does not eliminate professional motivation, workload constraints, supervision, or patient benefit.
hint: Separate the pay formula from a complete behavioral prediction.

title: Provider agency
prompt: A patient cannot judge whether an additional procedure is needed, while the recommending clinician earns a positive margin on it. Which economic concern arises?
correct: The clinician’s financial incentive may differ from the patient’s interest.
wrong: Information asymmetry is absent because the clinician is informed.
A positive margin proves the clinician commits fraud.
explanation: Expertise and payment incentives create an agency problem. The facts identify a potential conflict, not the appropriateness of a particular procedure.
hint: Identify who recommends the service and who can assess its value.

title: Induced demand evidence
prompt: A hypothetical area has more physicians and more visits per resident than another area. Why is that comparison insufficient to establish supplier-induced demand?
correct: Physicians may locate where underlying demand is higher.
wrong: More visits can only come from manipulation.
Underlying population health cannot affect visits.
explanation: Provider supply may respond to demand, and populations may differ in need. A causal claim needs variation that separates these explanations.
hint: Consider the direction of causality in physician location.

title: Quality measurement
prompt: A bonus rewards a hospital for a low unadjusted mortality rate. Which response could improve the metric without improving treatment quality?
correct: Avoiding patients with high baseline mortality risk.
wrong: Providing more effective care to the same patients.
Reducing preventable infections in the same patients.
Improving discharge coordination for the same patients.
explanation: Patient selection changes case mix. An unadjusted outcome metric can therefore reward lower underlying risk rather than better care.
hint: Can the hospital change who is measured?

title: Risk-adjusted quality comparison
prompt: Hospital A’s raw mortality is higher than B’s, but A treats patients with more severe conditions. What is needed before interpreting the gap as a quality difference?
correct: A credible adjustment or design addressing differences in patient risk.
wrong: A conclusion that A must provide worse care.
An assumption that severity has no relationship with mortality.
A comparison of hospital names only.
explanation: Outcome differences combine treatment quality and case mix. Risk adjustment can help, but its credibility depends on observed predictors and remaining selection.
hint: Compare outcomes for patients with comparable baseline risk.

title: Input substitution
prompt: A hypothetical clinic can deliver the same defined service and quality with either one physician hour costing $180 or two qualified practitioner hours costing $70 each. Which specified arrangement minimizes labor cost?
correct: Two practitioner hours at $140.
explanation: The alternative costs 2×70=140, below 180. Equal service and quality are assumptions of this exercise, not a claim about clinical substitutability generally.
hint: Compare total input cost for the same output.

title: Fixed and variable cost
prompt: A hypothetical clinic’s weekly cost is C(Q)=2,000+40Q, where Q is visits. What is marginal cost?
correct: $40 per visit.
explanation: The additional cost of one visit is 40. The fixed component affects average cost but not the derivative with respect to Q.
hint: Which term changes when Q rises by one?

title: Capacity opportunity cost
prompt: A clinic has one appointment slot left. Two hypothetical services yield net social benefits of $90 and $130, and use the same slot. What is the opportunity cost of selecting the $90 service?
correct: The forgone $130 net benefit of the other service.
wrong: $0 because no cash payment is required.
explanation: The opportunity cost is the value of the best forgone alternative, 130. The net loss relative to choosing that alternative is 40, a different quantity.
hint: Distinguish forgone benefit from the difference between options.

title: Prospective case payment
prompt: A hospital receives $8,000 for a defined case regardless of the case’s actual cost. If it lowers resource cost from $7,000 to $6,500 with quality unchanged, what happens to its case margin?
correct: It rises by $500.
explanation: The margin rises from 1,000 to 1,500. A prospective payment lets the provider retain this cost saving under the stated contract.
hint: Hold the payment fixed and change the cost.

title: Cost reimbursement
prompt: Under a hypothetical contract, a hospital is reimbursed every dollar of allowable cost and receives a fixed $1,000 fee. Ignoring other incentives, how does reducing allowable costs by $100 affect profit?
correct: Profit is unchanged.
explanation: Reimbursement and cost both fall by 100, leaving the fixed fee unchanged. This removes the direct retained-savings incentive in this simplified contract.
hint: Track the revenue change as well as the cost change.

title: Bundled payment boundary
prompt: A payer sets one fixed payment for surgery plus 30 days of follow-up. Relative to paying separately for each included service, what incentive does the bundle create?
correct: An incentive to reduce the provider’s total cost of services inside the bundle.
wrong: An incentive to maximize each separately billable service inside the bundle.
An elimination of incentives concerning services outside the bundle.
explanation: Payment no longer rises with each included service. Cost control may improve coordination or reduce useful care; the contract alone does not determine quality or behavior outside the boundary.
hint: Identify which services generate additional payment.

title: Coding incentives
prompt: A hypothetical case-payment system pays more for a higher recorded severity category. If verification is weak, which concern follows?
correct: Providers may increase recorded severity without a corresponding change in actual severity.
wrong: Recorded severity must equal true severity.
The system eliminates all documentation incentives.
explanation: Payment tied to reported categories creates an incentive to influence classification. This identifies a design concern, not evidence that any particular provider miscodes.
hint: Ask what information determines the payment.

title: Hospital market concentration
prompt: A hypothetical hospital market has shares 50%, 30%, and 20%. Using percentage shares squared, what is its HHI?
explanation: HHI=50²+30²+20²=2,500+900+400=3,800. Summing shares without squaring does not measure concentration.
hint: Square each percentage share before adding.

title: Merger concentration change
prompt: In a hypothetical market, hospitals with shares 20% and 30% merge, with all shares otherwise unchanged. How much does HHI rise on the 0–10,000 scale?
correct: 1,200 points.
explanation: The change is (20+30)²−20²−30²=2×20×30=1,200. This is a concentration calculation, not a full welfare conclusion.
hint: Subtract the two old squared shares from the new squared share.

title: Bargaining outside option
prompt: A hospital becomes harder for an insurer to exclude because subscribers strongly prefer access to it. Holding other bargaining factors fixed, what happens to the hospital’s bargaining position?
correct: It strengthens because exclusion becomes more costly to the insurer.
wrong: It weakens because subscribers value access.
It is unaffected by subscribers’ preferences.
It implies the hospital’s negotiated price must equal marginal cost.
explanation: A more costly insurer outside option can increase the hospital’s bargaining leverage. Actual prices also depend on costs, alternatives, and bargaining arrangements.
hint: Consider the insurer’s payoff if no agreement is reached.

title: Price competition and quality
prompt: A hospital market fixes reimbursement administratively while patients can choose providers and respond to quality. Which competitive margin remains possible?
correct: Quality and access can remain dimensions of competition.
wrong: Competition is impossible unless providers set prices.
All providers must choose identical quality.
Patient demand cannot affect provider behavior.
explanation: An administered price removes one choice variable but leaves other attributes through which providers can attract patients. The strength of that incentive depends on demand and payment.
hint: A fixed price need not fix every service attribute.

title: Pharmaceutical fixed costs
prompt: A hypothetical drug has a large sunk development cost and a constant low production cost per dose. What does marginal-cost pricing fail to guarantee?
correct: Recovery of the sunk development expenditure.
wrong: Zero markup over marginal production cost.
A price equal to marginal production cost.
Revenue per dose equal to its constant marginal production cost.
explanation: Marginal-cost revenue can cover production while leaving no contribution to sunk development costs. This is a dynamic financing concern distinct from use of an already developed product.
hint: Separate development expenditure from producing one more dose.

title: Average spending versus unit price
prompt: A hypothetical insurer’s spending rises from $100,000 to $120,000 while covered service quantity rises from 1,000 to 1,500 comparable units. What happens to average spending per unit?
correct: It falls from $100 to $80.
explanation: The ratios are 100,000/1,000=100 and 120,000/1,500=80. Higher total spending need not mean a higher unit price when quantity changes.
hint: Divide spending by quantity separately in each period.

title: Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio
prompt: In a hypothetical evaluation, program A costs $10,000 and produces 4 QALYs per person; B costs $16,000 and produces 4.3 QALYs. What is B’s ICER relative to A?
correct: $20,000 per QALY.
explanation: The incremental ratio is (16,000−10,000)/(4.3−4)=6,000/0.3=20,000 per QALY. Average cost divided by total QALYs answers another question.
hint: Use differences in both cost and outcome.

title: Strict dominance
prompt: In a hypothetical comparison, A costs $5,000 and yields 3 QALYs, while B costs $7,000 and yields 2.8 QALYs. Under a criterion favoring lower cost and more QALYs, which statement holds?
correct: A strictly dominates B.
wrong: Neither can be ranked without a threshold.
B is preferable because its cost per person is higher.
explanation: A costs less and yields more measured health. No positive willingness-to-pay threshold is needed to reject B under the specified two-attribute criterion.
hint: Check both cost and effectiveness directions.

title: Net monetary benefit
prompt: A hypothetical intervention adds 0.4 QALYs and costs an extra $12,000. At a stated threshold of $40,000 per QALY, what is incremental net monetary benefit?
explanation: Incremental net monetary benefit is 40,000×0.4−12,000=4,000. A positive value favors the intervention under this threshold rule.
hint: Value the additional QALYs and subtract incremental cost.

title: Quality-adjusted survival
prompt: For a hypothetical calculation with no discounting, a person lives two years at health weight 0.6 and three years at weight 0.8. How many QALYs accrue?
correct: 3.6 QALYs.
explanation: Quality-adjusted time is 2×0.6+3×0.8=3.6 QALYs. Averaging weights without respecting time gives the wrong total.
hint: Weight each interval by its own health-state value.

title: Discounting future costs
prompt: A hypothetical program incurs $11,025 in costs exactly two years from now. With a 5% annual discount rate, what is the present cost?
explanation: Present cost is 11,025/1.05²=10,000. Compounding instead of discounting moves the amount in the wrong direction.
hint: Discount once for each year until the cost occurs.

title: Evaluation perspective
prompt: A hypothetical program requires unpaid caregiver time but the payer does not reimburse it. Which cost treatment distinguishes a societal perspective from a payer perspective?
correct: A societal analysis includes the opportunity cost of caregiver time.
wrong: A payer analysis always counts every unpaid hour as a payer expenditure.
Unpaid time has no economic cost.
The societal perspective includes only billed services.
explanation: Societal costing considers resources regardless of who pays for them. A payer’s expenditure ledger can omit real time costs borne by households.
hint: Economic resources extend beyond paid invoices.

title: Budget impact and value
prompt: An intervention’s hypothetical ICER is below a decision maker’s stated threshold, but adopting it for all eligible people requires a large first-year budget increase. What follows?
correct: Cost-effectiveness does not by itself establish short-run affordability.
wrong: A favorable ICER guarantees no additional spending.
A large budget impact proves the ICER was calculated incorrectly.
Cost-effectiveness and budget impact are identical measures.
explanation: The ICER compares incremental cost with health gains. Budget impact depends on population size, uptake, timing, and expenditures, so a worthwhile intervention can still strain a budget.
hint: Distinguish value per health gain from total expenditure.

title: Extended dominance
prompt: Three hypothetical programs yield (QALYs, cost): A=(1,$1,000), B=(2,$4,000), C=(3,$5,000). If mixtures across identical eligible people are feasible, what happens to B?
correct: B is extendedly dominated by a mixture of A and C.
wrong: B is strictly dominated by A alone.
B has the lowest incremental cost per added QALY.
explanation: A 50–50 mix of A and C yields 2 QALYs at average cost $3,000, below B’s $4,000. B is not strictly dominated by either single program, but lies above the cost-effectiveness frontier.
hint: Compare B with a mixture delivering the same average outcome.

title: Sensitivity threshold
prompt: A hypothetical program costs an extra $9,000. At $30,000 per QALY, what minimum positive incremental QALY gain makes net monetary benefit nonnegative?
correct: 0.3 QALYs.
explanation: Set 30,000×ΔQ−9,000≥0, giving ΔQ≥0.3. This is the break-even gain under the stated threshold.
hint: Set net monetary benefit equal to zero.

title: Randomized program evaluation
prompt: In a hypothetical randomized study with complete follow-up and no spillovers, average spending is $2,400 among those assigned a program and $2,700 among controls. What is the estimated intention-to-treat effect on spending?
correct: −$300 per person assigned.
explanation: The assignment effect is the treatment-assigned mean minus the control mean: 2,400−2,700=−300. It is not automatically the effect among participants or compliers.
hint: Use assigned groups and retain the direction of subtraction.

title: Positive prevention externality
prompt: A hypothetical preventive action provides $40 of private marginal benefit and $25 of external marginal benefit at the current quantity. What is marginal social benefit there?
explanation: Marginal social benefit adds benefits to the actor and others: 40+25=65. External benefit alone is not the total.
hint: Include benefits that the decision maker does not receive.

title: Corrective subsidy
prompt: In a stylized market with no other distortions, a preventive action has a constant marginal external benefit of $15. What per-unit subsidy aligns private and social marginal benefits?
wrong: A subsidy equal to all private benefit.
explanation: A subsidy equal to the external benefit closes the private-social wedge in this model. Real implementation can involve additional fiscal and informational considerations outside the exercise.
hint: Match the subsidy to the omitted marginal benefit.

title: Public good properties
prompt: Once a disease-surveillance alert is broadcast, its producers cannot prevent anyone in the area from receiving it. One person using its information does not reduce its availability to others. Which properties are described?
correct: Nonexcludability and nonrivalry.
explanation: The inability to exclude recipients establishes nonexcludability; use without reducing others’ access establishes nonrivalry. A zero price alone would not establish nonexcludability. Producing the information can still be costly.
hint: Separate restricting access from depletion through use.

title: Horizontal equity
prompt: A policy gives equal access to people with equal health-care need regardless of income. Which equity concept does this most directly express?
correct: Horizontal equity.
wrong: Vertical equity through unequal treatment of equal needs.
explanation: Horizontal equity concerns equal treatment for relevant equals; here equality is defined by need. Vertical equity addresses justified differences among people with different needs or circumstances.
hint: Identify the equality criterion stated in the policy.

title: Vertical equity
prompt: A hypothetical allocation gives more services to people with greater medical need, all else equal. Which principle is most directly illustrated?
correct: Vertical equity based on differences in need.
wrong: A proof of maximum aggregate health.
explanation: Vertical equity allows appropriately different treatment for relevant differences. This allocation rule alone does not prove that aggregate health is maximized.
hint: Ask whether recipients differ on a relevant dimension.

title: Distributional weights
prompt: Two hypothetical programs cost the same. A yields 10 QALYs to group X; B yields 8 QALYs to group Y. A decision maker assigns weight 1 to X and 1.5 to Y. Which maximizes weighted QALYs?
correct: B, with 12 weighted QALYs.
explanation: A yields 10×1=10; B yields 8×1.5=12. The ranking depends on explicit distributional weights, not unweighted health totals.
hint: Apply each group’s stated weight to its health gain.

title: Financial risk protection
prompt: Two hypothetical policies deliver the same expected health and mean household consumption. One produces a mean-preserving contraction of consumption risk across illness states. For households with strictly concave utility of consumption, what additional benefit can it provide?
correct: Greater expected utility through consumption smoothing.
wrong: A guaranteed rise in mean consumption.
A reduction in every household’s premium to zero.
Proof that treatment quality has improved.
explanation: At the same mean, a mean-preserving reduction in consumption risk increases expected utility under concavity. The conclusion requires a risk reduction in that sense, not merely an arbitrary distribution change.
hint: Compare uncertainty as well as averages.

title: Catastrophic expenditure measure
prompt: A hypothetical study defines catastrophic spending as out-of-pocket medical payments above 20% of household income. A household earns $25,000 and pays $6,000. Is it above this study’s threshold?
correct: Yes; the spending share is 24%.
wrong: Yes; the spending share is 20% exactly.
explanation: The spending share is 6,000/25,000=0.24, exceeding 0.20. This uses the exercise’s definition; other studies may use different denominators and thresholds.
hint: Calculate spending divided by income.

title: Access beyond coverage
prompt: A hypothetical insurance expansion lowers patient fees, but the only clinic has no available appointments. What can be concluded about access?
correct: Financial coverage alone does not remove the capacity constraint.
wrong: The clinic’s supply must immediately become unlimited.
explanation: Insurance can relax a financial barrier while workforce or facility capacity remains binding. Effective access depends on both demand-side and supply-side conditions.
hint: Check whether an appointment can actually be obtained.

title: Equity and causal claims
prompt: A hypothetical dataset shows a health gap between income groups. What additional evidence is required to claim that raising income would close the gap by that amount?
correct: A causal design or assumptions identifying the effect of income on health.
wrong: Only the observed difference in group means.
Proof that the gap is statistically nonzero alone.
A relabeling of the health gap as an income effect.
explanation: Income and health can share causes, and health can affect earnings. A descriptive disparity is important evidence about distribution but does not identify the effect of an income intervention.
hint: Separate the disparity from the effect of a policy changing income.
